abstract: This study evaluated dietary betaine, alone or combined with vitamin C and/or sodium bicarbonate, in laying hens under chronic tropical heat stress, and characterized the intestinal morphological and microbial responses to the best-performing treatment. Two hundred forty 65-week-old Lohmann Brown hens were allotted to five diets (eight replicates of six birds) for seven weeks: basal diet (T0), betaine (T1), betaine + vitamin C (T2), betaine + sodium bicarbonate (T3), and betaine + sodium bicarbonate + vitamin C (T4). The mean temperature-humidity index was 29.68, indicating severe to very severe heat stress. T3 gave the highest hen-day egg production (89.93%) and egg mass (54.83 g), the lowest feed conversion ratio (1.85), and the lowest overall rectal temperature (41.20 vs. 41.57 Celcius in T0; p < 0.05). T3 was therefore compared with T0 for intestinal histomorphology and microbiota profiling. T3 increased villus height, villus width, and absorptive surface area in the duodenum and jejunum, and villus width and absorptive surface area in the ileum (p < 0.05). Microbiota responses were site-dependent: alpha diversity decreased in the small intestine but was preserved in the cecum, and beta diversity separated T0 from T3 at both sites. Aeriscardovia aeriphila increased at both sites, whereas Romboutsia ilealis, Bacteroides togonis, Enterococcus cecorum, and several Streptococcus species decreased or became undetectable. Betaine combined with sodium bicarbonate improved laying performance and intestinal morphology and was associated with a marked shift in gut microbial composition under chronic tropical heat stress.
